problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.statement: Given a list of non-overlapping, sorted intervals and a new interval, insert the new interval and merge any overlapping intervals. Return the result.
problems.understanding: The intervals are already sorted. Exploit that structure: everything before the new interval is untouched, everything overlapping gets merged, and everything after is also untouched. Three regions — three passes.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Append the new interval, sort everything, then run standard merge-intervals.

problems.intuition: The list is already sorted — no need to re-sort. Scan in three explicit phases: (1) intervals ending before the new one starts, (2) overlapping intervals that get absorbed into newInterval, (3) intervals starting after the new one ends.
problems.approach:
1. Walk while intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0] — append directly to result.
  2. Walk while intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1] — merge: take min of starts and max of ends into newInterval.
  3. Append the merged newInterval.
  4. Append all remaining intervals.

code.py:
class Solution:
    def insert(self, intervals, newInterval):
        result = []
        i = 0
        n = len(intervals)

        # Phase 1 — completely before new interval
        while i < n and intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]:
            result.append(intervals[i])
            i += 1

        # Phase 2 — overlapping: merge into newInterval
        while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]:
            newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0])
            newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1])
            i += 1

        result.append(newInterval)

        # Phase 3 — completely after new interval
        while i < n:
            result.append(intervals[i])
            i += 1

        return result

problems.takeaway: Pattern — Already-sorted list → Three-phase scan (before / overlap-merge / after)

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.statement: Given an array of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the resulting array.
problems.understanding: Once intervals are sorted by start time, any overlap can only occur with the previous interval in the result list. A single left-to-right scan is sufficient.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Repeatedly scan for any overlapping pair and merge them until no overlaps remain.

problems.intuition: Sort by start time. After sorting, overlapping intervals must be adjacent. Walk once: if the current interval's start is within the last result interval's end, extend; otherwise append fresh.
problems.approach:
1. Sort intervals by start time.
  2. Initialize result = [].
  3. For each [start, end]: if result is empty or start > result[-1][1], append [start, end].
  4. Otherwise: result[-1][1] = max(result[-1][1], end).
  5. Return result.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Sort by start → compare current start with previous end

problems.title: Non-Overlapping Intervals
problems.statement: Given an array of intervals, return the minimum number of intervals to remove so that the rest are non-overlapping.
problems.understanding: When two intervals overlap, greedy insight: keep the one that ends earlier — it leaves the most room for future intervals. This is the classic Interval Scheduling Maximization problem.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: DFS: try all combinations of kept/removed intervals and find the minimum removals.

problems.intuition: Sort by end time. Scan left to right: if the current interval overlaps the previous kept one, remove it (increment counter). If it does not overlap, keep it and update previous_end.
problems.approach:
1. Sort intervals by end time: key=lambda x: x[1].
  2. Initialize removed = 0, previous_end = -inf.
  3. For each [start, end]: if start < previous_end → conflict, increment removed.
  4. Else: keep this interval, set previous_end = end.
  5. Return removed.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Sort by END → Earliest Finish Time (keep the interval ending soonest to maximize future room)

problems.title: Meeting Rooms
problems.statement: Given a list of meeting time intervals, determine if a single person can attend all meetings (no two meetings may overlap).
problems.understanding: After sorting by start, any overlap can only occur between consecutive meetings. A single adjacent comparison pass suffices.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Compare every pair of meetings for overlap.

problems.intuition: Sort by start time. After sorting, any two overlapping intervals must be adjacent. A single pass comparing each meeting's start to the previous meeting's end is enough.
problems.approach:
1. Sort intervals by start time.
  2. Iterate from index 1.
  3. If intervals[i][0] < intervals[i-1][1]: overlap found, return False.
  4. Return True.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Sort by start → compare adjacent pairs

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.statement: Given meeting intervals, find the minimum number of conference rooms required to host all meetings simultaneously.
problems.understanding: When a new meeting starts, check the room that becomes free earliest. If it frees up before the new meeting starts, reuse it. Otherwise, open a new room. A min-heap of end times models this perfectly.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: For every meeting, count how many other meetings overlap with it.

problems.intuition: Sort meetings by start time. Use a min-heap to track the earliest end time among ongoing meetings. When a new meeting starts: if the heap's top (earliest ending room) is free, pop and reuse; otherwise push a new room. Heap size = rooms needed.
problems.approach:
1. Sort intervals by start time.
  2. Initialize rooms = [] (min-heap of end times).
  3. For each [start, end]: if rooms is non-empty and rooms[0] <= start, pop (reuse that room).
  4. Push end onto the heap.
  5. Return len(rooms).
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Sort by start + Min-Heap of end times (earliest available room at the top)

problems.title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
problems.statement: Given intervals and queries, for each query return the size of the smallest interval that contains it, or -1 if none exists.
problems.understanding: Sorting both intervals and queries lets us add intervals incrementally as queries grow. A min-heap ordered by interval size keeps the best candidate at the top. Expired intervals (those ending before the current query) are lazily removed.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: For every query, scan all intervals linearly and find the smallest containing one.

problems.intuition: Sort intervals by start and queries (with original indices) by value. Sweep queries left-to-right: push all intervals whose start ≤ query onto a min-heap keyed by size. Pop intervals from the heap whose end < query (expired). The heap top is the smallest valid interval.
problems.approach:
1. Sort intervals by start.
  2. Create sorted_queries = sorted((q, i) for i, q in enumerate(queries)).
  3. Initialize result = [-1] * len(queries), heap = [], i = 0.
  4. For each (query, original_index): push all intervals with start <= query as (size, end).
  5. Pop heap entries where end < query (expired intervals).
  6. If heap is non-empty: result[original_index] = heap[0][0].
  7. Return result.

optimal.title: Optimized Code (Python 3)
complexity: Time: O(n log n + q log q)

problems.takeaway: Pattern — Sort intervals by start + sort queries + Min-Heap by size (lazy-remove expired intervals)
